projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Gaston Connell was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Today is Sunday, July 28th, 2013. My name is Yvonne Fenner, and I'm here in Phoenix, Arizona, with Gaston Connell to conduct an interview for the Veterans History Project for the Library of Congress. Mr. Connell was a first lieutenant in World War II, serving as an army paratrooper. He was a part of the Battle of Southern France and the Battle of the Bulge and retired as a lieutenant colonel. And we're going to start way back at the very beginning if that's okay with you.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Let me add to that.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Lieutenant colonel in the reserves.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Because somebody could interpret that as I made a career out of it, the army, and I didn't want to do that.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay. Thank you for that correction. And then we're going to go to the very beginning, so can you tell me when and where you were born.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I was born April 18th, 1919, in Charleston, West Virginia.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: We're going to have a good story on how you got to the other side of the country, then.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: West Virginia isn't known for a good climate. It's beautiful in the summertime, but, oh, the winters are miserable.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Does it snow there?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yes, it does.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Were you an only child?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No, I had an older sister.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: How much older is she?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: She was four years plus.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What did your parents do?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I grew up on a dairy farm.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Oh. I grew up on a beef farm in Northern Minnesota. We're farm kids.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. I didn't appreciate it at the time, but I look back at it as really a very valuable part of my early childhood. The freedom, you know, I'm talking about the 19 -- the late 20s and the early 30s, before all the -- Japan's aggression started, put it in '35, '36, somewhere along there. And anyway, I just so fondly remember kicking off my shoes on Memorial Day and didn't put them on except to go to church till September. And, you know -- and I had the kids' dog, and the dog and I roamed the area. My parents never were concerned about where I was or my safety or anything. I was a country boy. I loved it.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: How big of an operation was the dairy?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: The dairy wasn't a big one. We had about, oh, 35 to 40 head of cattle, and maybe 25 of them were producers at any one time.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That's a big job twice a day.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yes, it is. I learned to milk cows early in my life. But then we got milking machines, but you still had to what they call strip them because the machine didn't finish the job. And that was my job much of the time.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I would imagine you learned hard work pretty early.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I always think of shoveling manure. I did it all.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That is your fondest memory, huh? I haven't ever talked to somebody that grew up on a farm that has one thing that they hate more anything else. One of my brothers hates fixing fence. I hate picking rock. Yours is shoveling manure.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Shoveling manure. You can't get much worse than that, I guess.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So did you go to school in West Virginia?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I did. I was fortunate. We lived in the county, and the County had its own school system, which my parents did not like. And they paid tuition for me to go to the Charleston school system, which was entirely independent of the County or the State. And I still remember they had to come up with ten dollars a month tuition. And ten dollars a month in the 30s was like a hundred dollar bill today, really.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: So I was allowed. You know, I've said that we were cash poor, but never went hungry. We always had lots of food and clothing. And, you know, I lived in overalls most of the time.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Yeah. So you went to grade school and high school?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I didn't go to kindergarten. First grade through 12, I went to the city system.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: When did you graduate high school?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: And then what did you do afterward?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Well, I -- during that time, I was one kid that read the newspaper. The Japanese were being aggressive toward China, and they took over -- I can't remember the province in Northern China. I'll think of it one of these days. And that, for some reason, it made a big impression on me and not a positive one. This is when the Japanese were not only invading China, but they were taking over all these islands, like the Solomons and the southern islands that many of them have -- Japan had no natural resources of their own, and that was one of the reasons they were reaching out and taking over places that had resources that they could use, not only for their population but for their military. The military was running the country. But -- and they were being very aggressive, and I could visualize that down the road, while the United States was telling everybody every day that they were neutral, there were many American citizens who were very much -- they had lived through World War I. My family, my mother and father did. And they -- it was still quite vivid in the minds of many people. It was in the news about Japan, and I, as I said, figured that eventually it was going to involve me. And they started the draft in probably 1938. But I graduated in '37, and the college I was going to go to did not have ROTC, but the army had this program, they called it CMTC, which was Civilian Military Training Camps. And that went for a month every summer. And a friend of mine and I decided we were going to take advantage of that. And it led to eventually getting permission -- I had to do a correspondence course and pass that before I could get my commission, but I got a commission as a second lieutenant in probably July or August of '41, just -- just before Pearl Harbor. And the day after Pearl Harbor, I went down to the military headquarters in Charleston and volunteered for active service if -- with one condition. I wanted to go to Fort Benning, that had an officers training course for three months of this. Very helpful to fill the gaps of what I didn't get in CMTC.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Was the CMTC full-time?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No, it was one month every summer for four summers.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: And so did you go to college around that, then?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. I was doing this every summer, and it didn't interfere with college. And I went to the junior college in Charleston, and then I went to Marshall, which now has become a university but it was just Marshall College when I went there. They're a small school in Huntington, which is maybe 50 miles away from Charleston.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did you graduate, or did you volunteer first?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I -- I volunteered. I was -- I think I was in the first semester of my junior year in 1941. And I went down and volunteered the next day.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did they take you up on your condition to go to Fort Benning?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yes, they did, thankfully. And also, the college gave me credit for the full semester, though I didn't finish more than a month. I got a break there. And at that time, you know, anybody in the military -- in the 30s, people respected the military. Now they spit on them.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: And, you know, that's -- you can imagine how that makes me feel.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Awful.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Because I have been involved or interested in the military ever since, since 1937. And seeing our U.S. Army go from a military to a Boy Scouts, that's -- that bothers me deeply because --

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I can imagine.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: -- we worked hard. I was -- one thing that I will never forget was doing -- we had to do a 25-mile march in eight hours in the summertime. And we were allowed one canteen of water, which is one quart, because they were teaching -- what do they call it, water -- well, it was trying to indoctrinate soldiers to be able to live on maybe a canteen of water for a full day because they might not have access to water. In combat, you -- you lived with what you had with you, including food. And that quart of water was pretty handy, you know. Occasionally you might find a civilian that would share some goodies with you, including water or whatever. That didn't happen very often because most of the civilians in the combat zone, they left. They abandoned their property. And I don't blame them because it's no holds barred when you got into a combat situation.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I'm going to make you go back to your enlistment one more time. So you enlisted in the army. Why the army versus navy or anything else, any particular reason?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: That was available.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay. That works.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did you go right to Fort Benning? Is that where you started at, then?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. I had these four summers of CMTC, and then I did go directly to Benning. And this was in January. I always thought of Georgia as being a southern warm state, but I --

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: A different point of view?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It was rainy and cold, and we were outside. We'd sit on these bleachers up in the side of the hill. And try to listen to a lecture wet when you're cold and shivering, it's pretty hard to comprehend what somebody is saying, but we muddled through it. And it was a good experience.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did you have what I -- what we call it now, basic training, so it was the physical part as well, or was it just the lecture part?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It was mostly classes.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay. Did you ever have to go through the physical training part?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Oh, not a real tough one till I went to the paratroops, and then they nearly killed me.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: We'll get there. So how long were you in Fort Benning for?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: For the three months.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Three months.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Then in April I went -- they split the class up, and the first half of the alphabet went to Fort Huachuca. That's how I ended up in Arizona.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Fort Huachuca -- do you know about Fort Huachuca?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I do not. I'm from Minnesota, and I live in California, so you'll have to tell me.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It's an old, old army camp. It used to be all black enlisted men with white officers. And they formed what was the cadre for a new division, which was the 369th Infantry Division. And they needed officers, so we went from Benning to Huachuca. They were bringing in these -- the division was not up to full strength, by any means, and so they were recruiting -- the army was still segregated, and they were recruiting blacks anywhere they could find them, and they were drafted. Most of the new recruits that I worked with were draftees, and some of them didn't even have a high school education. Some of them were only third grade, maybe sixth grade. I had one recruit that had an IQ of 37.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: And I was there for a full year. It was a good experience for me because they -- actually, the NCOs, noncommissioned officers -- the regiment had been there for years. Fort Huachuca was established, oh, way back in the -- probably -- they were fighting Geronimo. That must have been the late 1800s. And so that was the background for this fort, which it is right down -- are you familiar with either Douglas or Bisbee? You probably landed or transferred in one of them, unless you had a direct flight to Phoenix.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I got right into Phoenix.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: But anyway, they're old, old towns. Bisbee was a mining town, copper. There was a big copper pit there that is pretty historic. And you could go look at this pit that -- it must have been three or four hundred feet deep. It's huge. But you could see the veins of copper and stuff like that along the rim. But that operation had shut down, I guess, during the war.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So was that a training camp and you were officers that were training the enlisted men?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Fort Huachuca had been an old, established regular army post that had been in existence, and it was all black except for the enlisted white officers. And I was among the group that was sent out there from Benning. I didn't finish the -- Fort Huachuca is probably five or six miles from the Mexican border and maybe 50 miles west of Douglas, which is an old mining town, and it's right in the southeast corner of Arizona. And that was -- that and Bisbee, which was about 50 miles northwest of Douglas, was -- what was the mining company, copper company? I can't remember. But it had been just a company town, particularly Bisbee. And when I finished Benning, I think we got a two-week leave to go home and say, "Good-bye, see you when the war is over."

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: You went back to Virginia, then, for that leave -- West Virginia, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: West Virginia, yeah.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: How did you get out, then? By train?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No, I flew American Airlines from Charleston. And it stopped a few times. It stopped somewhere in probably Louisville, Kentucky, and Dallas. And we got off in Douglas, and we were totally on our own. Our assignment was to report at Fort Huachuca at a certain time. And we had enough time, but there was no regular transportation to Huachuca. So my friend and I, who I was fortunate enough that I had gone all the way through school from the seventh grade on -- we were in the same class, and we graduated together and went to CMTC together. And anyway, we got off the plane in Douglas because the next leg of the flight landed in Tucson, and Douglas was closer to Huachuca than Tucson. But finally we got a bus ride, I think, to Bisbee. And Bisbee is just a little town sitting on the side of a hill. It's very steep. There was the Copper Queen Hotel, which is -- I think it's still there. Had been there from sometime in the 1800s, late 1800s. And it was a very beautiful old hotel. And Jim and I went to the hotel, and we stood around the lobby looking for anybody that looked like a soldier who might know how we could get the rest of the way to Huachuca. Finally, a lieutenant colonel saw us wandering around with a dazed look, and he came up and asked us if he could be of any help. And we said, "Sure, if you know how we can get to Fort Huachuca." And he said, "Well, I'll be going there in a few minutes. You can ride with me."

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That's a pretty first-class ride.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That's a pretty first-class ride.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yes, it was. He was a real nice guy. So that's how we finally got to our assignment. And when we first got there, they were just beginning to get these recruits in, and we had the old army guys, who were mostly corporals or sergeants, but they had more -- much more practical knowledge than any of us new officers who had never been with troops before. And these guys were a tremendous help to us all the way.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What rank were you when you got there?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I was second lieutenant. And so I was really there all through the recruiting and training phase of these recruits. In the first place, they didn't want to be there.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: They were drafted, you said.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: And many of them were very inept. As I said, they hadn't had much education. Most of them had spent their lives walking behind a plow and a mule in Mississippi and Louisiana. And, you know, they were respectful enough, never had any problems there. Military, they didn't have any sense of the military or the purpose or what they were getting into. And my friend and I were platoon leaders, first lieutenants -- well, we got promoted to first lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That happened at Fort Huachuca?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: At Huachuca. And I decided that if I was going into combat, I really didn't feel very comfortable with having these guys, who were much better at fighting with a switchblade knife than with a rifle. So we wanted to get out of that regiment if we possibly could. And this was a priority regiment, we found out. You could not request a transfer from there to anyplace, just another regiment somewhere. You had to either go through -- request transfer into the air force or to the paratroops. So I couldn't see very well, so the air force was out, so I ended up in the paratroops. That's how I got there. That's why, but I really never had any regrets.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So where did they send you for that kind of training? That was --

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Benning.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Back to Benning?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Back to Benning. And that was a four-weeks, very intensive class. I can't remember exactly how it went, but we spent a whole week learning to pack parachutes, and we had to pack the parachute that we were going to use to jump our first jump.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Pretty good motivation for paying attention in that class.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: We did it right. The qualification was -- at the end was that you had to make five successful jumps. And that was -- I had no problem with those. They all went well. And graduated from there and --

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Can I interrupt you quick? I think you said that that's where they tied to kill you, so was there a lot of rigorous training there?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I spent literally four weeks of that training in very intensive physical endurance, climbing rock walls. And the thing that I will never forget is doing a jog completely around Lawson Field, which was the air base there. And if you dropped out on that jog, you were out of the paratroops. So I think there were maybe one or two people who did drop out in my group. But I was determined I wasn't going back to Huachuca or wherever, and I made it through. And I made my five jumps and got my paratroop wings, which Janice is wearing.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I saw.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: And -- oh, and the boots were almost as important as the wings, as you got to wear boots. And they always had to be so shiny you could practically shave in them. And, of course, you were expected to be exceptionally well presentable all of the time, dressed exactly according to regulations and all that good stuff. We were a very proud group, once we graduated from that class.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: There would have to be a real sense of achievement, getting through that kind of course.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yes. It's the greatest achievement I've ever achieved, physically speaking.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: When did you finish that? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It was -- well, it started -- in May. It was only a four-week course. I went there in April. And during that time at Huachuca, on the weekends, one of the fellas had a car, and we would drive to Tucson anytime we had a weekend that was free. And we set up our quote/unquote headquarters at the Santa Rita Hotel, and the guy there behind the counter always had reserved space for us. We were King of the Mountain, so to speak. And they had a beautiful ballroom, and they had big band music, live music. And somewhere along the way, one of the guys in the group we traveled with knew a colonel out at Davis-Monthan, and he lived off base in Tucson and had a daughter who happened to be a sorority sister of my wife, but she was the one who introduced me to my wife on a blind date. And that changed my life forever. I fell head over heels in love with that young lady. And we had several weekends together, and I probably spent a part of my leave time in Tucson’ I don't remember. But I'm trying to get the time lines straight here.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So you met her --

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: This is -- with great regret I left Huachuca and Tucson to go to parachute school. And after we finished parachute school, I was assigned to a training regiment.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Where was that at?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: That was at Fort Benning. Benning is right outside of Columbus, Georgia. It's about 50 miles south of Atlanta. It's right on the river that divides Georgia from Alabama. It was the Chattahoochee River. We had training camps or training areas on both sides of the river. And this was quite a big river, and we had these amphibious vehicles we could ford across the river. And one big incident that I remember, the vehicle had a drain plug in the bottom of it. One of the officers ended up sinking in the bottom of the river. Why I would remember that because I had nothing to do with it, but it was funny. Then I also had a very sad and disturbing incident there. I lost my commanding officer in a night -- was it night? It was a night parachute jump over in Alabama, training camp. And we had a training regiment, which I don't know what you know, but the makeup of most army regiments is usually four battalions. And I was assigned to one of these training battalions, and I had -- somehow I ended up being second in command. Because I really wasn't experienced enough to hold that office, but I got it anyway. Well, I ended up being the training officer and made up the training schedules and that kind of stuff. I had this lieutenant colonel who I worked with very closely and was a terrific gentleman. But on this night jump, we jumped, and his chute never opened. And that -- it was fatal. And that was the only fatal jump I remember until, of course, in combat. That's another story.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Do you know what year or how old you were when you were in that position?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: 1943. Yeah. It was later that year my wife, Jean, decided to join me, and we got married. We were married on the post at Fort Huachuca by the post chaplain whose name I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What was the date for that one?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: November 6th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay. Did she come back with you to Georgia then, or were you moving again?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Well, we were pretty soon assigned -- or at least I was -- to go to overseas. And I went overseas when we were only married five months. But we went up to -- I think we had a couple of weeks' leave. And when I went back to Georgia, my wife stayed in Charleston with my parents, and I went to Fort Maryland, which was a station where they equipped the troops to have the equipment and everything they needed to go overseas. And I think I had some notes. Sailed for Europe on April 25th. That was 1944. I really had a cook's tour because I went over on a brand-new navy transport, and they said we had a total of 5,000 troops onboard, but I was what they called a casual. I was on orders, but I didn't have any -- any troops or anybody with me, wasn't a member of an organization. And it landed. They had a camp there where people were processed for further possible combat duty.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: How long did that sail last, the trip across?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It took nine days. Because this was one of the first shipments that went over without an escort. We had a brand-new navy transport, which was very fast. And we took nine days to cross the Atlantic, into the Mediterranean.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What was the accommodation like onboard?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: You know, I can't even remember. But with 5,000 troops on that -- I think the officers had better quarters than that, and, frankly, I do not remember.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Okay. It wasn't of importance, then. There's nothing memorable there.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No, it wasn't, that you would remember, particularly.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So you landed in Oran?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: You landed in Oran?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: And they processed you, or what happened then?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: We were there maybe four or five days, and we shipped off to -- from there to Naples. And these were all paratroopers, paratroop officers mainly. And we ended up in a camp up in the mountains that was in the process of sending officers who came in to fighting units. This is -- I don't know if you remember Anzio?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It was one of the -- it was a sad, sad business. We ended up pulling out. Our objective was to get to Rome, but we didn't get off the beach. We were going first to Anzio as replacements, but, no, they sent me down Sicily to another training camp. And Sicily, you would never believe, they were still using these big two-wheeled ox carts, oxen pulling the thing -- not horses, oxen. In fact, they had a trolley in this little town called Trapani, T-r-a-p-i-n-i, something close to that. It was small, unimportant town on the Mediterranean. And that's the first time I really got a good look at the Mediterranean at sea level, and it was the bluest thing I could ever remember. Sort of reminds me of the blue of this picture up here.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Beautiful.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: And I was there for four or five weeks and back to Naples.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What did you end up doing in Naples?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: This was another center for reassignment. And I was assigned to the 509 Parachute Infantry Battalion. It was the only one in the service. And it had a history going clear back to North Africa and Sicily and -- but they had been assigned to North Africa, and I think they were not there for the initial invasion, but they were assigned the mission. We were close to the border between Italy and France, right in that area. It was clear down to the Mediterranean. And our assignment was to make sure that the Germans didn't come over that area. So, actually, it was very quiet and peaceful and beautiful country. And it was what I call a piece of cake as far as assignments were concerned. You don't get those very often. And we were there clear into late November. And I'm sorry, I'm going to have to excuse myself for a minute.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Sure. [Break taken.]

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: We were back in Naples. It was the 509.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No, I was assigned there to the 509. I had already been in Southern France. [Side discussion.]

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Oh, I went to Naples as a replacement. I was with the 509 Paratroop Infantry Battalion. I tried to tell you they went all the way through North Africa I believe from England I think all in combat gear. And they couldn't -- couldn't get up and walk around. I can imagine. They jumped from the German-held -- over German-held air bases so the ground troops could get there. And then they went on to take another one or two air bases. They went on one or two jumps in there.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: And what --

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I can't remember whether they jumped in Southern France or went in by ships. I went from Naples to Marseille. I guess, just close to Marseille. We landed on the beach there.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did you parachute in?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No. We -- I never made a combat jump. I had a total of 15 jumps in training situations. Coming in from Southern France, all the action from Normandy was all going north and east, so toward Belgium. And we were pretty well-situated just to the west of the German border.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Do you remember the timing of it then? We're still in '44.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It would have been September '44. But it took that long to -- the trip from Naples to Marseille, you would think it would be about 12, 15 hours. It took us two days. We were using these little landing craft. And there were a bunch of enlisted men down in the hold. About 50 percent of them were seasick. It was a miserable trip for them. Fortunately, I never got seasick. A lot of people did. They could just think about riding in a boat and they'd get sick just thinking about it. Anyway, Naples -- oh, I think we covered Sicily, didn't we.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: That was a very interesting assignment because you had the feeling that it was early 19th Century out there, earlier than that. They had this trolley in town that had a track, and the car was pulled by ox.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That must have been so strange, coming from the U.S. You must have felt like you were going back in time.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I really was. Unfortunately, I didn't get to know the natives. That would have been a great treat, but we didn't quite have the opportunity to mix much with the population. But it was a beautiful assignment. It was like a vacation, almost. We weren't training very hard. There was nothing that was memorial in the way of training. I do remember training in Trapani, which is clear out in the northwest corner of Sicily. And I'm trying to remember the names of the city where you go from Sicily to Italy, where you cross there. Anyway, the train trip to Trapani to where you embarked back into Italy, I got to ride in the engine. And that was -- it wasn't a big engine like we have with our later rail. Somehow the engineer invited me to join him in the cabin. And I can remember the firemen shoveling coal into this big boiler and how 19th Century it was. It was just astonishing. The things you learn about what goes on in other parts of the world is just amazing. Anyway, I joined the post just northwest of Nice, which is a coastal resort town and had beautiful hotels. They had a trip for the post. We were assigned to this 509 unit whose mission was to see that the Germans or Italians didn't cross the border into France. And they had the -- the Germans had -- well, anyway, this is a leg of the -- Pyrenees? Anyway, the mountain that we were watching had a huge barracks that had been occupied by the Germans. And my first combat experience or first time I ever got shot at, I was assigned to take a patrol because they hadn't seen any activity in the top of the mountain for three or four days, and they were wondering if the Germans had pulled out. So I was assigned a mission to take this patrol around the side of the mountain to try to figure out if there was anybody still up there. And they were there. That was the first time I ever got shot at, and they opened up on our patrol. And we -- there was snow on the ground. And we were, of course, not going to engage them. Our mission was to get back to our established camp. And I can remember rolling down this mountain. The snow was too deep to walk or run in it. So I put myself down on the ground and rolled down the mountain. And I remember the troops did the same, and we ended up back in our friendly lines with no casualties. But I did get shot at. I remember that first shot. It went whistling over my head. That's something you never forget.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I can imagine. That would stay with you.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. Anyway, eventually the 509 was withdrawn from there and sent up to a camp outside of Paris. And we were -- it was a beautiful setup. Most of the officers were quartered with the population. Families would take in one or two officers. I'm sorry I can't remember the name of the town. It was a typical French small town. And the people were very friendly to the U.S. because we had liberated them from the Germans. Anyway, we were settling down there to have a nice little rest camp for a couple of weeks and all of a sudden the Battle of the Bulge broke out, and that put an end to our vacation plans or leave plans very quickly. The whole battalion was loaded up in trucks and headed north. And, unfortunately, the truck I had, most of my -- I think I had my platoon. No, it must have been two trucks because they wouldn't all go in one truck. But the truck that I was riding in was not a -- most units had their own motor company, and they had trucks available, but our battalion did not. And this was -- the trucks were from some motor pool where they had drivers assigned to the vehicle. Anyway, the first thing we had -- our truck had a flat tire, and we had to drop out of the convoy. And fortunately, the driver, who was black, he was a competent driver, and he knew how to change the tire, and we got back on the road. And we got -- the closer we got to the Bulge, the more nervous he got. And finally he said, "Sir, I ain't going to drive no more," so I had to take over driving the truck. And we were out of the convoy. We were driving alone. And by some miracle, I finally caught up with the rest of the unit. And I can remember these roads were almost as narrow as our road you find in our forests. Not well-traveled. We were getting into mud and everything else when we finally got there and caught up with the rest of the unit, who were stopped and were camping.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What time of year was that?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: That was early December or mid-December, I guess, 1944.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I imagine it was pretty cold.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: It was cold. It was cold. Snow on the ground. It was mushy. It was not hard frozen.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Were you tent camping?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I'm sure we were, but I don't really remember that part of it, for some reason. Anyway, somehow our battalion was assigned as infantry following a tank company. You'd follow -- take your group and follow along behind the tank. And I can't tell you much about the action we engaged in there. I cannot remember the tank fire. True combat experiences, for some reason I just cannot recall the details. Again, this was another patrol that we had a pretty good-sized group. I don't remember exactly, but we had one tank. And we had a major in command. I guess he was from the tank company that we had been attached to. I don't know much about him, but we went to go to find out where the Germans were because we had no action, no activity from them. And so we were patrolling again down these little dirt roads to see if we could find the Germans, and we finally found the Germans, but there was no exchange of fire. We came up to the intersection and went down a little dirt road, and there the Germans were right in front of us with the road blocked off, backed up by tanks. This was not a match for us. The major decided he would disable this tank and we would take off on foot, get back to our friendly lines again, somewhat the same situation but involving tanks. But I think everybody survived that. Oh, we ended up being surrounded. That's why we destroyed the tank. The Germans moved in behind us after we had approached their position, and they had cut off the road. That was when it was decided that the tank could not retreat, get past this roadblock on the way back. So we were sort of -- the foot troops were given direction to -- you're on your own to get back to our friendly line.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Was that challenging?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: We weren't quite to the border with Southern France, because we didn't get fired on. It was rough terrain. I do remember that. I was very happy -- we had to come down and into the friendly lines. And of course we were happy to get back. This, incidentally, was Christmas Eve, which was just another day as far as we were concerned. I think they tried to give us a hot lunch, but I can't remember if that was successful or not. Mostly we were eating K-rations or C-rations. They were not very satisfying, but very high in protein and all the nutrients. But in taste, not so good. But if you're hungry, you'll eat most everything.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: If it's that cold and you're moving around, I imagine any food would be good food.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So you made it back to camp.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: To our -- oh. We went on, pushing them back across the Rhine River into their own country. And then, I guess it was the end of February, we decided to just abandon our 509 company battalion because out of about 750 total troops, there were 37 people still active, able to do whatever. And not all of the rest of them were casualties in the sense of being killed, but many of them were out because of frostbite or other illnesses. And there were a lot of casualties. I don't recall exactly, but out of 750, there were 37 officers and men left to the 509 battalion. So after our mission of getting the Germans pushed back across the river, they decided to disband the battalion rather than try to leave supplies with the troops. And what was left of us was assigned to the 508 Infantry Regiment, which was part of the 82nd Division, which was very famously noted for their accomplishments in combat, all the way from Normandy on. I joined them in February of '45.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Had you seen active combat through that whole period, then?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. We were -- I think I had a nine- or ten-day leave somewhere in there. And I got around to Paris. Paris was deserted. The streets were deserted. People were hiding. Not a very notable trip, the lack of activity in Paris, which has always got a lot going on.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Was that a little bit unnerving?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Hm?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Was that unnerving?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Sort of, yeah. A lot of the restaurants and those places were open. I can't remember where we were -- or where I individually billeted, but I guess we were on our own in a hotel, as I recall. This was actually leave time. You would think Paris would be the ideal destination, but at least it was not a combat zone.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That was the main thing, to get a break.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: On other interviews, they talk about time on and time off, but when you're in a combat situation, I would imagine it's a 24-hour situation.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Of course, you're not constantly in a firefight. You might get into a firefight, and it may last most of the day and into the night. Usually it quiets down at night. But you have to be on your guard for patrols out from the enemy. They're always active probing -- and we are too -- probing to see where we are. And get the notion of weaponry and getting tanks or artillery are always very important things to scout out when you're patrolling, the men and the territory. Anyway, I was with the 508. I was the weapons platoon leader with the 508, and I do not have that written down anywhere, but that's what I recall.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: What does a weapons person do?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: This was a company that had heavy machine guns. They were water-cooled, .30 caliber machine guns. And the infantry used small, .60 millimeter mortars, but the weapons company has the .81 milliliter mortars, and they're just like artillery. They're very, very high explosive stuff and can do a lot of damage. But frequently, a lot of the company were trying to take your machine gun rods and plant them in different parts of the line, separate from sometimes the mortars, because the mortars are usually back behind the hill from where you are, out of sight from the enemy. And so my job was just to check on them, on the various supplies, and see that they were taken care of.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I would imagine you saw a bit of destruction with that, then.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I bet you saw a bit of destruction if you were with the --

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. We were going up the Rhine River, a combat area, had some heavy fighting along the way. We got almost just south of Cologne, with a K, and we were relieved and went to the rest camp. And where we went from there, I don't know. Anyway, in May -- we had been in combat since April, as I recall. In May we were in a rest area. And on VE Day, combat was ceased. And it was really colorful. Part of the 82nd Division, we were given the choice -- the 82nd had been designated to stay in Europe as Eisenhower's honor guard. And you had a choice of staying with the 82nd or going to the 101st, which at that point was in Berchtesgaden, which was Hitler's redoubt, Hitler's hideout, and doing nothing. But they were -- their assignment was to be redeployed through the U.S., go to the Pacific area. So you had a choice of staying in Europe or going to the 101st with a chance to go for at least a month in the U.S. to be reoutfitted to be shipped out to the Pacific. I had a hunch that the war in Japan would be over before the 101st ever got there. I thought it was a pretty good hunch, so I went to the 101st. But we stayed in Europe, this was May. I joined them early in June, and we went from Berchtesgaden, which was a piece of cake, and left there in June. And we were assigned to go to a little town in Austria, which is called Bad Gastein. And it was a little town, a tourist destination where Churchill used to go for his vacations. And that's what it was noted for. But we ended up in this nice hotel accommodations. And I was assigned to the main headquarters in some capacity, which required nothing because the war was over. And I was assigned two sergeants to assist me to do nothing.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: A tough job.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. Some of the rewards. Anyway, that was an easy assignment. It lasted -- well, I left there in November, because my number had come up to go home. And I can't remember just how the number system worked. It had to do with the number of months you had spent in Europe. And my turn came up, and I was eager to get home and see my bride of five months.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: How were you -- were you able to stay in touch with her?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. I've got a foot locker tray full of letters that she wrote. And I wrote when it was possible, but that was not very often. But she wrote almost every day.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Were you able to receive them?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: We would get a whole bunch of them at one time. And I have a watch that is really no longer serviceable that she sent there. That was our first anniversary present. [Dog barking, side discussion.]

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So she sent you a watch for your first anniversary?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: And you got it.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: And I got it in the combat zone.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Amazing.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I still have the watch. It's been rebuilt a couple of times since then, though it's not very serviceable. It runs about four hours, and then it quits. It's an old wind-up. They didn't have battery watches in those days -- maybe there were, but we didn't have them.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: But you got letters from your sister and your parents or just from your wife?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I got letters from my parents. My mother used to send me postcards self-addressed back to them, and that worked out pretty well because I could give them a short message of some kind and drop it in the mail, and a month later they'd get it. That's about the way the mail worked.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Anything memorable about the time off that you had recreation-wise? What did you do to pass the time when you had down time or the easy assignments?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Well, I think that one leave time that I got, I went to Paris. And I was very disappointed because of rations, there was just very little business going on. But the restaurants and the hotels were doing pretty well too. As far as general commerce, there was not much going on. It wasn't a very memorable vacation, walking the streets of Paris, and there were very few people there. I can still remember the Champs-Elysees where the Arch of Triumph is, and it was -- in this area, it's all pedestrians. And to see it almost deserted, it just felt unbelievable. But it was. And the population was there, but they were all holed up in their homes, didn't go out. As I said, there wasn't much commerce. I guess soldiers on leave kept Paris in business.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So did you get to go home in November?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: My number came up in November, and I was shipped to Brooklyn from Brussels, after going through all of the inspections. They wanted to make sure you weren't taking any of their army armament home with you, guns and pistols and stuff, which were quite coveted, as you might imagine. A lot of them got through, but I did not. I had nothing, really, except an old .38 caliber revolver that I don't even know how I came into possession of it because it was not an army issue or a German issue. It was made in Germany, but it was something I picked up. I really wasn't interested in bringing home any mementos of Europe. I was happy to leave and go home to my bride. I boarded an old Liberty ship in Brussels. Those old Liberty ships were put together during the war in the Atlantic, and they were shipping goods to both England and Russia. And they didn't have enough commercial vessels that they would commandeer, so we had the midsized freighters built on the assembly line put into service, and some of them were still active after the war, and that is what I came home on. And I boarded the ship in Brussels, and it was November, and the sea was rough. And we could see the southern coast of England for three days, it was going that slow. It took us I think 21 days to get home. I landed in Philadelphia and got a train to -- my wife drove to El Paso, and I took a train to El Paso, and we met up there. I can still remember the train coming into the station in El Paso and looking out the window, and there was my wife running alongside the car. So that was a reunion really of great magnitude. I had -- when I was in Fort Benning, I borrowed $500 from my parents to buy a secondhand Studebaker. That was one of the best cars I ever owned. And it had been well cared for, I don't know how, but I bought it from a person.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Hold on a minute. I'm going to flip the tape over. [Interruption in recording.]

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Here we go.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Oh, I bought it in Georgia, when I was in Columbus, Georgia. It was the little town next to Fort Benning. And my bride and I had five months together before I was assigned to camp. I was there three or four days and then boarded the ship for Oran, came full circle, I think.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: That's amazing. What kind of reception did you get coming back?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Well, of course GIs from the army were well-respected and treated like kings in most places. It was a great reception, not only privately but by the community. They appreciated the soldiers, which that was the exact opposite of the poor guys who were in Vietnam. They would come home and get spit on, called baby killers and all kinds of stuff. I just can't imagine. It was not like the reception we got. We could do no wrong.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So did you get out of the army at that point?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I -- well, I had leave time built up, and so I was off of active duty. I still had leave time which took me clear into March of '46. And I was getting full pay. Another thing about the paratroops, if you went into the paratroops, you were paid one hundred dollars a month. And I was -- my wife was -- when I went overseas, I designated a certain portion of my income to go to her while I was out of the country. And, you know, I just kept 75 dollars to buy beer and stuff like that. And one of the things I'll never forget in combat, the officers every week were given a carton of cigarettes and a fifth of tequila, which was a great bargaining unit. I can still remember nylon stockings being the mode of trade in Europe because they just didn't have those kinds of luxuries. They were considered a real luxury, nylon stockings. They were a premium. The German soldiers would buy them and cigarettes. I remember a lot of captured Germans being so delighted to get American cigarettes. I didn't even smoke -- well, I did. I guess I did smoke a little bit, but not a carton a week. Maybe a pack a week would be more my style.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: So you ran out of leave in '46.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Hm?

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: You ran out of leave in the spring of '46.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Then what happened?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I went into the reserves. And then I joined the Arizona National Guard. And I worked for them through the rest of the 40s. Oh. Well, I had reached the rank of major, and when I finished university -- I've gone backwards. I need to go backwards a little bit. When I got out, I had the GI Bill, which paid for school.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Where did you go to school?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: University of Arizona.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: You came back to Arizona then.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. My family was unhappy, but I decided I was going to live in the West.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did you come to Phoenix?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Tucson. That's where my wife was. We'd been married for five months. Well, by that time it was a year and five months, but we -- okay. Somewhere around there, in '46, I got out. I was still going to school. I had the opportunity -- I think I said I was -- when Pearl Harbor came along, I was in my first semester junior year at school. And when I came back, I transferred into the U of A and finished my BA degree there with a major in economics. I soon found out you couldn't do much with a major in economics as far as getting a job, so that's why I decided to go back to school again. I was 31. I did not find the brokerage industry very lucrative, unless you had control of some money, a hundred thousand dollars or so, and that didn't happen. And then I went to work for Sears, worked there for a year in the hardware department. I was just a salesman on the floor, and I hated it. I didn't like Sears. They -- you know, I can't say that they didn't treat me well because they did, but the whole retail market did not appeal to me. So I decided to -- one of Jeanie's friends, my wife, had a sorority sister in college who had married a GI who was in pharmacy school at the U of A, and this was a new school that started in 1950, I guess.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: When were you there?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: At U of A, I went back to get my pharmacy degree. I felt I needed to have a trade that was valuable.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: When did you finish that?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: 1953. I went two full years and two summer schools, as I recall. Of course, I had a lot of courses already that they required that I already had. And I had -- something the dean of the college -- remember it was just a new college, just started, and I had gotten to meet him somehow, and I was a couple years older than he was, the dean of the college, and he let me petition out of some courses like physics, which you couldn't prove that I had any need for. What else? There was another couple courses he let me petition out of. And I got a job with a drug store. It was a local chain, not very progressive. When I graduated, there was a group in Phoenix that really had started up in Superior or someplace like that. So I came to Phoenix and went to work for them and spent the rest of the time in Phoenix.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: And then you said that you were in the National Guard at that point?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Yeah. Anyway, I had been fortunate enough to have a commanding officer that promoted me from captain up to a major, but when I moved to Tucson, they had a National Guard unit, but all the major assignments were already filled, so I had to drop out of the National Guard, and I went to the reserves, which was a collection of individuals, not an active unit, but they had classes, continuing education classes. I participated in that for my not active duty, but kept in the reserves as a retired.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: How long were you in the reserves for?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Until 1955, when I -- I think I was 65, and you had to retire. And I retired as a lieutenant colonel.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I have three last questions for you.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: One is have you had any contact or did you keep in contact with any of your fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No, because I had never really formed any real friendships, except I do have somewhere these two sergeants that I found. The people to assist me, did nothing.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Did you ever join any of the veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: The second to the last question is how would you say your wartime experiences really affected your life? Or any life lessons learned.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I grew up in the service. I was a kid, a Good Time Charlie, until I got into the service, and I had to grow up. And it was really in that respect my military service was very beneficial to me. Of course, I was double lucky because I came back alive, particularly after the Battle of the Bulge, which was wicked. Fighting the enemy, I survived that and cold, wet, snowy weather. But I survived. Actually, December and January went by, and the elements were much kinder because it was springtime. It was livable. But we were still in combat till April, as I recall, of '45. Then the war was over and I had to -- {Dog barking.]

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Any great life lessons learned or should we call it a wrap?

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: I had matured in the army because I had to. I had troops I was responsible for, and I had to get with it pretty quick. And at the end I survived.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: Well, I'd like to thank you for your time today. We put this piece of history in, another piece of the puzzle. And thank you for your service.

sp.speaker: Gaston Connell
sp.p: Well, I appreciate that. You know, it's very kind of you. If I'd have never been in the service, I would never have met my wife. My mother wanted me to stay in Charleston and marry some socialite, which was not very interesting to me.

sp.speaker: Yvonne Fenner
sp.p: I'm going to go ahead and shut this off. [End of recording.]
